blocks.x: Albert Nicol is talking. London, February 9, 1967. Just for the record, Albert, would you like to tell us your time and place of verse?
I was born in New Orleans, May the 27th, 1900.
Can you tell us something about your training and taking lessons and so on?

Well, I started taking lessons around 9 years of age with my uncle, Wooden Joe Nicholas. He was my big influence on this jazz scene. And later on, I went to Papa Teo and took lessons with him for about a couple of years. Then Lorenzo Teo, his son. And finished up with him until around 1915. Then I started to go pro. My first gigs around New Orleans was with the Maple Leaf Band. Then Buddy Petite's Band. When Jimmy Noon left to go to Chicago, I played with Buddy Petite and several other bands around New Orleans. In fact, nearly all of them until 1917. And I went to Navy for three years during World War I. Studied a little bit. Played in the Navy Band. And came out in 1919. In December. Played with Buddy Petite again. And then formed a little group of my own. With Barney B. Godd on tenor we were learning in Saxton. And Louie Russell, Paul Barberin, Willie Santiago, Alnorma Twai on trumpet. And spent a year or so at Anderson until King Oliver sent for us to come to Chicago. And stayed with them, with King Oliver until 1926, August. And went to Shanghai, China with Jack Carter. The latest note, Terry Weatherford, Billy Page, Frank Etheridge. And had a wonderful year at the Plaza Hotel in Shanghai. Afterwards, instead of coming back to America by the way of California. We got our transportation. Mine was until Marseille, France. I was on my own afterwards. But anyhow, I was stopped in Egypt and India and Singapore, Sumatra, Malay. And finally arrived in Marseille in October 1928. Went to Paris and stayed a week waiting for my boat from Schilberg to go to New York. Had a wonderful surprise, seeing Sidney, my old sidekick.
Sidney Bechet.

Sidney Bechet. We came up together since we were kids in New Orleans. He was playing at the Shea Florence in Marmota. And it was a nice reunion, he and I, for a week or so. And I came back to New York, October 1928. Joined Larry Russell's band in 1929, beginning of the year. And stayed with that band until 1940. 1940. Which was a very pleasant experience and one of the best bands I've worked with. That was the band that we toured with Louis. It was supposed to be Louis Armstrong, but it was Louis Russell featuring Louis Armstrong during the 30s. I got out of the band in 1933 for about six months or so and played with Chick Webb at the Savoy. Came back with the band, with Louis Russell. And then left the band in 1940 and then I got tired of making these one-nighters. I played all over the street. Played with John Kirby's band. Took Buster Bailey's place for a few months. And played with all the small groups on 52nd Street. And went to California in 1946. Played with Ori for a while. And freelancing, I had the pleasure to play with Jack Teagarden and all the rest of the gang out there in California. And was house man at the hangover club on Bush and Powell in San Francisco for two years. And got enough of that sunshine out there and thought I'd like to come back east. Which I did. In April 1953. A couple of months later, I had an offer to go to France from Delaunay. Sidney Bechet spoke about me and recommended me to Delaunay. He corresponded for a while. In October 1953. I came to Europe. On a two months contract. To play with Reviata's band. At Club Padido. The two months passed so quick. And instead of coming back to America, I had offers to see the continent. And I took advantage of it. Went to Switzerland, tour, Germany, Austria, Italy, Spain. And it was 57 before I came back to America. Stayed seven years. And came back to the States. It was nice to see my old friends and relatives. In New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Francisco again. And after three months, I got homesick for Europe again. So I came on back and I'm over here. Very happy. Anything else? Yeah.

Like I was in your early days when you were first starting up playing. Yeah. The guys you used to listen to most. Oh. Have perhaps influenced you? Many. The guys from the Kings. Particularly Clare. Well, I tell you. When I was a kid, 14 years old in New Orleans, I used to go up on Sundays to hear Kid Orris Band. He was playing at Miss Coors Lawn. It was a penny party in those days for the kids, you know.

And I used to go up on Sundays to hear Kid Orris Band. And he was playing at Miss Coors Lawn. 10 o'clock at night. And Johnny Dodds was playing with Orris and he really amazed me. He was my idol at the time. Johnny Dodds gave me a lot of enthusiasm, you know. Enthusiasm. Yeah. Yeah. And of course you had all-fine musicians at that time. afternoons until 10 o'clock at night. And Johnny Dodds was playing with Ori and he really amazed me. He was my idol at the time. Johnny Dodds gave me a lot of enthusiasm, you know? And of course you had all fine musicians at that time. Big guy, Louis Nelson was in his prime, young man playing plenty of horn. Picou was in his prime. Teo was in his prime. George Baquette was one of the finest too. Great, great clarinetist. And a few others. So I had all those guys to listen to and influence me. When did you take up saxophone? I had taken up saxophone around 1921 in New Orleans. I was playing at Anderson's as I said. And Bonnie took up tenor and I took up alto. And two of the years I've played all the saxes. I've played alto with King Oliver and tenor in China. Came back to America and played alto with Louis Ross's band for a year or so. Then they switched me on tenor, first tenor. I played baritone and doing all the clarinet work. You played all the saxes? All the saxes, yeah. Because in the 30s, you see, you had to play
in the reed section, you know. I'll switch off for a minute. Would you like to talk about your experiences with symphony orchestras over here?

Well, I was in, after I left Shanghai, as I told you, I went to Cairo, Alexandria. I mean, Cairo, Egypt, for six months, playing at the Shepherd's Hotel. And you had, we had a band of all the nations, we called them, because we had Greek. Papas, he played third alto in a band, and he also played classical music, also flute, double on flute, classical group. And the five hotels on Sundays, from eleven to one, they would play for tea like, you know. Tea dance. Yeah. And we'd form a symphony. All the guys doubled, you know, these musicians in Europe at the time, they were all great musicians. And so after being there six months, when I went to Alexandria, Egypt, at the Casinos in Bacchus, my instrument got out of whack, my Albert system clarinet. I had to send it to Paris to have it fixed. And Italian, Mr. Bonomi, who was playing clarinet in the symphony, he had two clarinets, and he loaned me his bohem. In fact, he taught me the rudiments of the instrument, and he gave me a lot of points in classical training. Had you been on Albert's system before, up to this point? Up to that point, yes. And then a couple of months, when my horn came back from France, well, I had forgotten all about the training. I'd forgotten it, but it seemed strange to me. In fact, I loved the other system much better, and it did me a lot of good. Then on Sundays, on, as I said, rehearsing with the band, they had me on third clarinet, playing third part sometime, but in the second. And by the end of the year, I was coming on pretty good with this type of music. And it was a wonderful experience for me, from when I came back to the States, playing different arrangements. You found it improved your reading and everything? Oh, it improved everything, sure. Playing and everything, reading and everything. That's right. Disappearance of reading. Yes, it was a good thing. Very good. Good training.
Did you hear much of Jimmy Noon in the old days?

I heard Jimmy Noon when I was a kid, 15 years old. As I told you, he was playing with the Young Olympia Band. In fact, we were taking lessons together with Papa Teo also. Jimmy was a couple of, about four years older than I am. And he was playing a lot of clarinet. And it was Jimmy. Bonnie came after me. Bonnie Begarde studied with Teo also. And Omar Simeon in Chicago, studied with Teo. And Teo was in Chicago. Now, Jimmy was one of the best. When he left New Orleans to join Charlie Cook's band. And when we heard him in 24, when I came to Chicago with Bonnie and different ones, when King Oliver sent for us, Jimmy Noon was about the greatest. Because Bonnie and I, every night when we get through playing, when Jimmy was playing in the after our place open around two in the morning. And he was our idol. He had improved so much. And to me, he was the greatest in those days. Yes, I know Jimmy very well. It was a pleasure to hear Jimmy. And of course, I heard him again just before he passed away. He came to New York and he played several times in different places. We copied a lot from Jimmy. Bonnie and I both. We got a lot of
acquaintance from him. Would you say he was a real original?

I should say he was an original. Jimmy Noon was a great musician. And sure, he had his own sound. Because we copied a lot. Benny Goodman's got a lot of things from Jimmy Noon, a lot of guys. The only guy that played different from all of us, I'll be truthful, was Johnny Dodds. He had something different from all of them. I don't think he's taken any lessons. He learned in another way, but it was so beautiful. This guy played a lot of horn, man. He had his own sound, his own fingering and all. I wonder how he did it sometimes. Tone was different. Everything. He was a jazz man, original jazz man.
Did you ever hear the original King Oliver Creole jazz band in about 22, 23, with Johnny Dodds and Dewdry at the Lincoln Gardens?

I took Johnny Dodds' place in 24. I knew King Oliver when I was a kid, around New Orleans, playing second trumpet in the brass band with Manuel Perez, an onward brass band. Then I played with King Oliver a couple of times before I went into the Navy, when I was around 16 and 17 years of age. Joe was in his prime then. He'd play these bonkés and things like that and balls. Sure, I knew all the old times, but in 1922, I was in New Orleans. I didn't hear them at the Lincoln Gardens. When we came up there, it was in 24. But I heard of the band. In fact, I knew the whole band. They're all from New Orleans.

There are a lot of different theories as to why King Oliver asked Louis to join him. A lot of people say that he was scared of Louis, and that he thought that if he had Louis in his own band, he wouldn't be cut. Do you think this is true?

No, I don't think it's true at all. You hear all kinds of funny rumors later on about jazz musicians. King Oliver sent for Louis because it was the Spentonese band. He wanted to change to get out of this New Orleans six-piece deals. He wanted to build his band up to what he did, to an eight or nine-piece band. It gets sort of modern-ish at the time, you know, with reeds. And Louis was the greatest thing in New Orleans when he sent for Louis. He wasn't doing Louis a favor. Louis was on the boat with Fade Marble. And I heard that when I came out of the Navy, I was amazed with what I heard, because Louis was cutting everybody. So when the king sent for the Navy, he had him on second. And once in a while, Louis would play first, you know what I mean? And Louis was making a name for himself at the time, but he was a great musician coming up young.

You were talking about Armstrong, Albert. Yeah. And remember you saying the other day that you thought that Louis got a lot from Bunk and those more recent records made in American music by Bunk, you didn't feel were really Bunk in his prime. Obviously they weren't because he was getting on years. Could you tell us a bit about Bunk? You heard Bunk in New Orleans.

When I first heard Bunk, I was a kid around nine or ten years old. He was playing with the Superior Band. Maggill was playing with the Imperial. Bunk was the radiest trumpet player at that time in New Orleans, what we call Gut Bucket later on. He was a kid around nine or ten years old. He was a writer. And Bunk had ideas. It's too bad that they weren't recording in those times. This man was really great. And I heard the old man again in 45, after being in retirement for 20-some years, and 60-some years of age. He made a remarkable comeback. But that wasn't the same Bunk I knew. No.
Would you say that that band that was recorded in 42, 43, 44, the Bunk band, it was the same as Bunk was playing around about 1918?

The style was the same because he got all the old musicians to play that style, like George Lewis and his guitar player. His old man used to play bass. What's his name? Schlerdragpa? No, no, no, Morera. Lawrence Morera. Yeah, I know his brother John and Simon were the two greatest string men we had. He played with the Young Olympia Band in 17, 18, 19 and 20 like that. Morera was a kid. He was a little younger than I am. He was small. His old man was a hell of a bass player. And when they got this band for Bunk, George Lewis was playing on this old style, as real New Orleans, as authentic. He had never left New Orleans, you know what I mean, to play in other styles. And it was really an old New Orleans thing. It was wonderful to hear someone still playing it, you know what I mean? Because we didn't hear it in New York and Chicago. These guys were playing something else.
I mean, I think along those lines, you have the Sam Morgan Band, Jim Robson recorded in the 20s, and Louis Domaine's band recorded.
Yeah, I know.

Now to me, Louis Domaine's band, in its style sounds very similar in some ways to King Oliver's band, what King Oliver was doing in Chicago. Yes. But really, what you're saying, Albert, is that Bunk's band of the 40s was going back in style to prior to the... Prior to the 20s.
Prior to the 20s.
Yeah, prior to the 20s.

That's just exactly what I'm saying. Now I'll give you another one. A lot of people think New Orleans had one style of music. No. You had different sounds. You had guys that played just as the music was written. You understand? Yes. You had musicians that played arrangements. Then you had small groups like Buddy Petit, Bunk Johnson playing something else. You see, like you have now, today. You have bands, we call them commercial bands now. You have the studio bands and the radio and TV. Wonderful musicians playing arrangements. Then you get small groups that are playing what they feel. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. And I admired, because Dodds was way ahead of us in his ideas, in his playing. He was matured. And it was something that you didn't learn in the method. And even I'm from downtown, you see. You take Piku, you take Teyo, they played beautiful jazz but it was mostly of a classical thing. You know what I mean? Playing right and all like that. But they didn't play Gut Bucket like, or had a little Gut Bucket band uptown. Buddy Petit had one downtown because they used to buck each other all the time. You see that's a different thing. Sam Morgan had a nice little group at the time. They were playing what they felt and what they knew. But you had other musicians playing harder stuff, what we called, because we weren't matured to that yet. We were playing original New Orleans stuff that we heard.
And when you started having lessons, you started to read straight away?

Did you? Well, I had to. No, no. Yeah. Papa, he gave me lessons a few months before he let me play the horn. He wanted me to get the rudiments of the music. Because he said, you've got plenty of time to learn this jazz. He used to call it ragtime then. There was no such thing as jazz when I was learning. He said, you've got plenty of time for that. Learn those notes. And he says, one note played right is better than two, three dozen notes all jumbled up and what not. He said, that's not music. I want you to learn right. And which I'm very happy that I had that training. My greatest kick, something I'm going to put in my memoirs. I saw an old man, I went back to New Orleans in 39 and I saw a lot of the old timers there, you know, with Louis for about five days. We were with the big band, the Louis Russell band. We had a 16 piece band and four trumpets with Louis and three trombones and I was playing the first tenor. We had four saxes in the band. And a wonderful band for arrangements. And also we could once in a while for intermission play a few of these numbers, New Orleans numbers, you know. And it was a pleasure to see the old timers who I knew when I was a kid coming to the band. But they weren't playing anymore. They figured they were old, you know, they were grandfathers and things like that. And of course most of New Orleans musicians they had another trade. Cigar makers and carpenters, bricklayers, plasterers, they played music mostly on the side for their pleasure. So they weren't playing anymore. And it was nice to see them around. They came to hear you. They came to hear me and tell us how good we were. You know, how we came up from kids, you know, just starting out. Now we were pros, you see. And of course you heard Kid Reno. We were talking about Kid Reno the other day. We came up together.
Kid Reno was the first one. That's another one. He was a creator. Kid Reno was the first one making high notes.

Louis started making high notes after Kid Reno. He was inspired by Reno. Kid Reno was, he never left New Orleans. He was just, he was happy with New Orleans, you know what I mean? But in the 20s, Kid Reno was playing plenty of horn, man. He was really blowing.

Could we talk a little bit about the rhythm sections in those days? Yeah. You said that the Bunk band in 44 was a hark back to the old style prior to 1920 because Bunk hadn't played for those years. Yeah. Would you say that the rhythm section, that was Baby Dodds, Slow Dragon, Lawrence Marrero, Elton Purnell, all came later. Would you say that that rhythm section was similar to the ones before 1920?

I will say it, yes. You know, they had the original beat. I'll be truthful with you. I didn't hear any bad rhythm sections from New Orleans. Even now, I don't think they have this thing, it's a natural. They get to our bass and drums and things, they play together. They play for the other guys. They didn't do a lot of solo work, but they played together. It was a beautiful thing. They didn't blast or nothing in those days, you know. It was full. We didn't need a piano. No.
It's the timing. It's the- They had rhythm.

They were born with it. It seemed like- Well, that's another thing. I don't remember having to practice no rhythm. I was practicing notes because it was a natural thing. We walked in rhythm and little kids, five or six years old, hum a tune, they hear a tune, played by a band on the corner, and the next day they're all whistling. It was a natural thing. I didn't know you had to study rhythm and all that stuff until later on through the years. We have to, you don't.

That's who you have to do the study. So the changes, Albert, in the rhythm section have only really come, you think, in the New Orleans men, the change came with the equipment more than with their basic approach. I mean, they got, when they probably moved from New Orleans and there's different sorts of cymbal and things came in, naturally they would introduce those into their kit and that would be another sort of variety of sound to the whole thing.

That's right. Yes. You see, even your musicians, when I left New Orleans, I thought it was that type of music all over the world. And I was disappointed when I heard a lot of great musicians playing dance music, you know. Yes. They were playing without that beat, what you call a beat now, you know. Yes. They were playing with notes, but they weren't swinging. And they didn't have it in them. Now, the music has changed quite a bit and has improved quite a bit. And to prove it, when I first came to Europe, I've heard some of these young groups, 10, 12 years ago were copying records. Now, I hear them on the air, if you don't tell me who they are, I can hardly tell if they're from the States or where they're from. They got it down now in England, in Scandinavia, in Italy. All these little groups out here, sit with them and play with them. They're playing like natural. There's no more amateurs and nothing like that. They got it. And especially in the modern, it's hard to tell. In Sweden and in Scandinavia, those cats are really blowing, man. You can't tell who it is, you know what I mean? Unless they tell you. You see them in person and this guy is talking Swedish and playing American. Shoot, man. Something else, you know. That's the truth. Right here in England, man. I heard some groups on BBC in Paris, listening, because I always catch this program. There's a small group with clarinet, vibes, piano, bass, and drums. And at first, I thought it was Buddy DeFranco on clarinet or something like that. And here it is, British. And I said, hey, what is this? You know what I mean? It is low. It used to be that you could tell the difference. No, you can't. A stranger is a lot.
Do you think the same goes for European rhythm sections? Because I think this is where we tend to fall short of the American.

I heard, that question has been asked before. You got some of these bands don't have a solid beat, you know. But you take these pros that I was, like I told you about this BBC thing that I've heard with the small group. That cats has got nothing but rhythm show. Drummers, oh, come on. There's no more bad drummers in a good band, you know what I mean. I heard a recording date the other day in the studio here, right here in London. And man, them cats was really playing. There was no Max Roach or nothing like that. He was playing himself and he was swinging.
Who was it?
I don't know his name. They told me his name and I forgot. All I know, that band sounded great. Studio band.
Going back to the old days for a moment, would you like to tell us a bit about Jelly Roll more?

Well, Jelly, he's my favorite. Jelly Roll was something else. He was a character. A lot of people, youngsters ask me about Jelly Roll. They got the wrong impression of Jelly, I think. Jelly was a great musician and a great person, but you had to know him, you know. If you met him the first time, you might think he was very arrogant, because he did speak what he thought. You know, he was outspoken. But one thing I'll say about Jelly, he spoke the truth. Whatever he said, he meant it. He was truthful. And if you played, he would tell you to play. If you didn't, he'd say, you just don't play, man. So a lot of guys didn't like him for that. He was too outspoken. But afterwards, even when he passed away, they said, hey, you know something, man? This cat was great. Because I heard a lot of musicians that knew Jelly, used to pan him, you know, say, oh, Jelly Roll, he just talked plenty. But Jelly could prove what he was saying. He'd get on that piano and prove it. He was a great composer. I've never heard Jelly sound bad. There were a lot of places he would, he was very arrogant. He wouldn't play on 52nd Street, because the guy used to kid him and say, hey, Jelly, why ain't you on 52nd Street, man? He said, because they can't pay me. And he may not have a dime in his pocket, but he was that type of a fellow, you know? And principles.

Oh, he did. But don't you think he suffered because he couldn't adapt himself to playing in the 30s? His style was so rigid. Huh? His style was so rigid that he couldn't fit into the music of the 30s.

Jelly could play any type of music, man. Jelly was just himself as a person. Jelly was a musician. A musician can play with anybody. You know what I mean? If you're a musician, and Jelly was a musician, it was a lot of guys couldn't play with him. He had a certain thing he wanted to hear. And his type of music that he loved was the New Orleans type. He was very happy when he played with New Orleans guys, because he got what he wanted. You know what I mean? And that's what a lot of these guys in the East didn't like Jelly for, because they couldn't swing. See? Swing?

That's right. Well, not the sort of swing you know. Why do you think that Jelly didn't have very much influence on musicians that came after him? Whereas other pianists, like Earl Hines, had tremendous influence on them?

Well, Jelly was a different person from Earl Hines, you see. As I told you, his thinking was different. Jelly was a great musician, but he wasn't commercialized. Jelly had two or three bands, you know what I mean? Coming up in the early 30s. And he just didn't care about going through all these headaches, to build a band, to continue on. He figured his name was there. He was Jelly Roll Morton. He was different. He was just a different, he was a character, as I said. Money didn't mean nothing to Jelly. He was a hustler. He was a gambler, you know, and things of that sort. Like you say, well I can't even drink so much, man. And he was no big drinker. I've never seen Jelly Roll drink. I heard he drank later, but I've never seen a man drink, take a drop of liquor. He was serious about his music. But he knew what was happening. Because I've seen him at the rhythm club in New York. He sat behind all of them. James P. Johnson, Fats Wallace, Spitt the Lion. Jelly was arrogant. Duke. I've seen him ask Duke, come on and sit down and play a little bit. And Duke wouldn't follow that. Duke had his band at the cotton club. Great musician.
Duke was being quoted as saying that he thought Jelly was a very bad musician.
Well, I don't know, probably. But I didn't think he was a bad musician. His records are right here to prove it. I love it. Diggy sounds, diggy sounds, he's original. I think he was a great musician.

Well, to move to another great musician, a great band of musicians, when you were with Louis Russell, you must have had a tremendous, you were nine? Nine of us there. How many years were you there? Ten years. A little over ten years. Getting back to another musician from New Orleans or just outside, Henry Red Allen, you must have played a lot with him in those years, with the Louis Russell band. He was with them what, four years?

I was in the band when they sent for Red from New Orleans. I was in the band when we sent for him, yes, when he came to join Louis Russell's band. And you had so many good bands in New York at the time, organized bands, and we were just one of another band. But we had an original style of our own, because Duke even told Louis Russell, you must always keep that style.
But I mean, when Louis Armstrong and Red Allen were in the band together, did they each take solos together?
No, Louis was being featured as Louis. Nobody can follow Louis. Louis is the greatest. But we had another book to feature Red.
I see. You see?

Yes. It was well balanced. We had three trumpets as I said, three trumpets in the band. When we play, when Louis is on, we play his arrangements behind him. We're featuring Louis. And the next set probably we feature our band. And Red would come on and take over.
Louis would just come on and do an hour or so. He would do his spot and then the band would play over.

But if they play together, which they have, well they play together, we had arrangements where you were Red. But I tell you one thing, if it was something in unison, and with the three trumpets and Louis together, Louis would make the rest of them sound like little boys. Really? Oh yes. Oh yes. We have arrangements to prove it. Alexander's Ragtime Band. Heart full of rhythm. Get the big band. And you hear Red and all of them, they sound like little boys. Yes.
Well it just shows how fantastic Armstrong was at that time. Because you hear records like Feeling Drowsy and Swing Out, which Red Allen featured on those. Very nice. Very tremendous.
Very nice.
And to think that Louis could go here.

Oh man, Louis blew them all into bad health. I remember one time in New York on Rudy Blesher's program, This Is Jazz, and Louis was a guest star for that Saturday. And Bill Davidson was on that program. And Louis played two, three numbers with the group, with our regular group. And when Pops took over, Bill Davidson sounded like a little boy amateur. And he couldn't play it no more the rest of the evening. He was so nervous. Because he didn't have the sound. The master was there, man. That's something else. You don't have no, you only have one Louis. And I'd say you had one Bechet. You see what I mean? You had one Dodds. These are outstanding people, man. Nobody sounds, you know, when they're on a session with you, I'm sorry. You don't have to the problem.
Could I ask you, Albert, you heard Buddy Bolden when you were a child. And I wonder if you could remember at all how he sounded and how the band played.

Well, I've had the pleasure to hear Buddy Bolden when I was a young lad, around seven, eight, six years old, something like that, the first time. He was playing at the Lincoln Park uptown. My Uncle Joe used to take me up there on Sundays. It was a matinee thing in the open air. And I've heard him two, three times. I wasn't impressed with him or nothing at the time because I wasn't interested in playing. But they had so many bands and Buddy Bolden was just another trumpet player to me. But I've heard Buddy Bolden. And I've heard him the last time, I think I was around eight, nine years old. He was in the brass band in New Orleans and he was playing. And it surprised me after coming up to be a young man to hear so much talk about Buddy Bolden, Buddy Bolden, and Buddy Bolden. He had so many trumpet players, you know what I mean? But I did hear the man, yes.

This is what I think, you know. Just my feeling about it is that there couldn't have just been one band that started the whole of the jazz ragtime thing off. There must have been lots of other musicians around that time.

There were so many at the time. You see, but Buddy Bolden was one of the pioneers of the ragtime. I will say that. He was playing a rather style of music. But at the time when I heard Buddy Bolden, I heard Bunk Johnson, as I told you, to hear him often, you know, and these balls. I was living right around the corner from the Perseverance Hall on that end, and between Durban and Erkwart. That's right. And so he didn't impress me too much at the time, you know. It's amazing now how they're making a legend out of Buddy Bolden and about him playing all that loud. Now I'll tell you another thing. Later on, at the fairgrounds, in 1921, in 1920, you didn't have all these cars making noise at night. You know, you didn't have any vehicles running. It was quiet. And in the summertime, King Oliver, when he was playing at the fairgrounds, we could hear, I was living several blocks away, you could hear the sounds of wind with caroties. You could hear the bass drum all the time, boom, boom, boom, boom, and things like that. But you could hear the little faint sounds, and I could understand what they were talking about. Always to hear faint marble from the river. If the wind was blowing our way. From that calliope. Because that's the time my parents would tell me, it's nine o'clock boy, come on, get ready, go to bed. You hear that calliope?
You see what I mean? What was the calliope? Was that a boat?

That's that thing like an organ by steam. Fate used to play this thing when they come in, leaving the river to go on a tour, then coming back, the last thing he played is calliope. And it would sound all over New Orleans. See?
It was quiet then. You used to take the band off the boat?

No, no, the band stays on the boat. He's playing this thing on the boat, by the river on Canal Street, on the head of Canal Street. And these sounds would go all over, you know what I mean? The city was quiet.
Was this before he started playing, when he ended playing?

That's the end and when he began. He just played this thing as a come on thing. Yeah, he played the piano with the band. And when they put it, he put it on his raincoat and this thing was full of steam.
And Fate was the only one who could play this thing. It was sort of an advertisement.
It was an advertisement for the boat. No, that let you know that the boat was in, it was nine o'clock.
Yeah, come on folks.
Yeah, yeah, it was a thing like that. And they'd leave around seven at night, you know, to make this two up the river. Yeah. Down the river, rather. That's rather nice.
Can I ask you a little bit about vocalists in the twenties? Did you hear much of Bessie Smith?

Oh yes, I've heard Bessie Smith and had the pleasure to play behind her for a week. When I first came to Chicago to John King Olive, we played in the theater on 31st and State. Those times you didn't have any microphones. And I played a week with her. And later on in 25, she came back to Chicago to do something with Clarence Williams. And they used some of our band. They used Louie. She used Louie. She used Paul. She used me. And who else was it? I think it was Bud Scott to play behind her, to sing, you know, for this big ball. It was the Elks place on Michigan Avenue. About two, three thousand people in this place. And Bessie was something else, man. She had a sound, you know. Yes, I've heard Bessie Smith several times. And played with her twice. Behind her twice. Not in the records or anything, but just on a session.
Did they say that she used to drink rather a lot? Probably she did.

I don't know a person in her life. I wasn't interested in her life. All I know, I played the gig with her and I've heard her. And I've heard her several times through the years in the theater, paying my admission to go sit down and hear what she's putting on. She was one of the greatest blues singers I think existed. I don't know nothing about a person in life. I don't know anything about Bessie.

No, but one reads that she always used to go for a recording session. She used to be stank on sober for a recording session. But often, in public performances, live performances, she used to be a little bit the worse for wear over the time she got on the stage.
Well, I don't know that. I've never seen her other than on the stage singing. You know, I don't know anything. Not backstage. And I don't know nothing about it.
She goes to live for dear fit out with us Europeans?

No, I tell you, I'm glad I made the trip in 59, because my relatives were bugging me about when am I coming back and things of that sort. And I felt sort of self-conscious and I should go back and see what's happening and see my people, you know, and see the gang, all the musicians. So I did go back and with the thinking I would be away indefinitely, probably six to seven months. But after I arrived in New York for the first week and saw the gang, you know, and heard them, I went to Chicago and heard some sounds in Los Angeles, heard some sounds, San Francisco, back to Chicago. And I really got homesick for Europe. And I was convinced that Europe is for me, you know what I mean? I have adapted myself that I'm more at home in Europe than I am in the States. Truthfully. Well, that's good. That means you're happy. So I'm very happy over here and I have friends all over the continent. I know all the groups. Every major city I go to, I know the vans, I know my friends. So I'm at home and I'm very happy.
You don't feel homesick or...
No, no. No, no. No, never. I don't get lonely or nothing. I'm happy. Very happy over here. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Opening and birth in New Orleans
segments.summary: Interviewer opens the recording in London, 9 February 1967; Nicholas gives his birthplace and date.

segments.title: Career summary from lessons to the Oliver band and Shanghai
segments.summary: Nicholas recounts lessons with Wooden Joe and the Tios, early bands, the Navy, his own group, King Oliver in Chicago, Shanghai and the trip home.

segments.title: Reunion with Bechet, Luis Russell band, California and Europe
segments.summary: He meets Bechet in Paris, joins Luis Russell until 1940, then plays New York, California and moves to Europe in 1953.

segments.title: Early idols: Kid Ory's band, Johnny Dodds, and taking up saxophone
segments.summary: He heard Ory's band with Dodds as a boy, names clarinet favourites, and says when he took up the saxophones.

segments.title: Symphony work in Cairo and Alexandria
segments.summary: After Shanghai he played Shepheard's Hotel in Cairo and Alexandria, doubled in a symphony group and learned Boehm clarinet basics from Bonomi.

segments.title: Jimmy Noon as idol and influence
segments.summary: Nicholas studied with Noon under Tio, heard him again in Chicago in 1924 and says he and Bigard copied him.

segments.title: Johnny Dodds's originality and knowing King Oliver
segments.summary: Dodds stood apart in sound and fingering; Nicholas replaced Dodds in 1924 and knew Oliver from New Orleans brass bands.

segments.title: Why King Oliver sent for Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: He rejects the rumour that Oliver feared Armstrong; Oliver wanted a bigger band and Louis was the best in New Orleans.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson in New Orleans and in the 1940s comeback
segments.summary: He heard Bunk as a child and again in 1945; the 1940s band kept the old style, with George Lewis and the Marrero family.

segments.title: Different styles of music in New Orleans
segments.summary: Bunk's 1940s band returned to pre-1920s style; New Orleans had arranged bands and small hot groups, Dodds ahead of them.

segments.title: Lessons with Papa Tio and the 1939 return to New Orleans
segments.summary: Tio made him learn notes before playing; in 1939 he saw old-timers who had other trades while touring with Russell.

segments.title: Kid Rena and the New Orleans rhythm sections
segments.summary: Rena made high notes before Louis; Nicholas says the old rhythm sections had a natural beat.

segments.title: Changes in rhythm and European groups today
segments.summary: Equipment changed but the beat did not; he finds young European groups now play indistinguishably from Americans.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton as a person and musician
segments.summary: Nicholas defends Morton as outspoken, truthful and proud, a musician who loved New Orleans players, and is not a bad musician.

segments.title: Red Allen and Armstrong in the Luis Russell band
segments.summary: Allen was sent for from New Orleans; Armstrong was featured separately from Allen in the band's book.

segments.title: Armstrong's dominance over the trumpet section and guests
segments.summary: Armstrong made the other trumpets sound small, as did a radio appearance where a guest trumpeter faltered beside him.

segments.title: Hearing Buddy Bolden as a child
segments.summary: He heard Bolden at Lincoln Park as a young boy, was unimpressed, and doubts the legend built around him.

segments.title: Fate Marable's calliope and the quiet New Orleans night
segments.summary: He explains the steam calliope on Marable's riverboat, heard across the quiet city at nine o'clock.

segments.title: Bessie Smith
segments.summary: He played behind Bessie Smith in Chicago, including a 1925 ball, but knows nothing of her private life.

segments.title: Why he prefers living in Europe
segments.summary: He visited the US in 1959 but became homesick for Europe, where he has friends in every city.
